clue.text: Wine, small drink to which some guys are attached

definitions.text: to which some guys are attached

parts.note: tent is a deep-red Spanish wine, an old crossword favourite
a peg is a small measure of spirits, especially a brandy or whisky and soda

explanation.surface: A glass of wine and a nip of spirits that some men have grown attached to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guys' are not men here but guy ropes, the lines that hold a tent taut and are pegged into the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Guy ropes are staked to the ground by these, so it is the thing guys are fastened to.

clue.text: Time enough, perhaps, to make stout

indicators.note: signals that the letters may be reordered into another word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Given long enough, something can be made strong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges T and ENOUGH; 'stout' suggests beer, but here it means sturdy.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something stout is to strengthen it, making it sturdier and more robust.

clue.text: Isle of Wight features almost unnecessary?

indicators.note: the synonym stops one letter short of complete

parts.note: needless means unnecessary

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some landmarks off the south coast are almost pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: The Needles are chalk stacks off the Isle of Wight, an island off England's south coast; 'almost' drops the last S of NEEDLESS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Needles are a famous row of chalk sea stacks at the island's western tip.

clue.text: Best black lead

parts.note: a plum job is the best one
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: The best dark pencil lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' suggests a pencil, but here it is the metal: a plumb is a lead weight.
explanation.definitionFit: A plumb is a lead weight on a line, and the word comes from Latin plumbum, the metal.

clue.text: Driving course with game associations

parts.note: golf is a game
links are connections or associations

explanation.surface: A road with sporting connections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving course' suggests a driving school, but it is a place where golfers drive balls.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf course is where players drive off the tee, so it is a course for driving.

clue.text: Two-seater wedding conveyance, going by air?

definitions.text: Two-seater wedding conveyance, going by air?

parts.words: Two-seater wedding conveyance, going by air?
parts.note: recalls the song Daisy Bell, with its marriage proposal and a machine built for two, which rides on pneumatic tyres, so it goes along on air rather than through it

explanation.surface: A couple's wedding transport seems to be an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going by air' suggests flight, but the joke is that this machine runs on air-filled tyres; the song Daisy Bell gives the two-seater and the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: The tandem of the old music-hall song is a pedal machine for two riding on inflated tyres.

clue.text: Bristling, hard at work around hospital

indicators.note: the word for occupied goes round the abbreviation

parts.note: busy means hard at work

explanation.surface: Someone bristling as they work hard at a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Bristling hair or a beard is thick and shaggy, standing out stiffly.

clue.text: Ganymede as holder of trophy?

definitions.meaning: in Greek myth the Trojan youth Ganymede served wine to Zeus and the gods
read literally, someone carrying a prize cup

explanation.surface: Ganymede pictured as the winner holding a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Ganymede was carried off by Zeus to pour wine on Olympus; read as two words, the answer is also anyone carrying a cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A cupbearer pours and serves wine; the phrase also literally means one carrying a cup.

clue.text: So long a toast at Number 10?

parts.note: a cheer can be a toast, a raised glass and salute
the figures 1 and 0 look like the letters I and O

explanation.surface: Saying goodbye with a raised glass at Downing Street.
explanation.walkthrough: Number 10 Downing Street is the British Prime Minister's residence; here 10 is just read as I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerio is a British informal word for goodbye, as is so long.

clue.text: Self-regarding sorts chewing stogies

indicators.note: chewing mangles the word stogies, rearranging its letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Smug people chomping on cigars.
explanation.walkthrough: A stogie is a cheap cigar.
explanation.definitionFit: Egoists are people focused on themselves, putting self-interest first.

clue.text: Ill-matched with a French peer

parts.note: un is French for a
a peer is an equal, someone of the same standing

explanation.surface: A badly suited pairing involving a French nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' suggests a lord, but here it means someone of equal rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Things ill-matched are not on a par, lacking balance or parity.

clue.text: Boss well-versed In Morse, it turns out

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other, the clue putting the expert word into the shuffled code name
suggests the letters of the code name come out in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
to be up in a subject is to be well-versed in it

explanation.surface: Someone in charge is an expert in Morse code, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it turns out' rearranges MORSE to SREMO, and 'In' puts UP (as in 'up in a subject') inside it after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A supremo is the person in overall charge, an informal synonym for a chief or head.

clue.text: Hayseed for a mountain goat

parts.note: a hill stands loosely for a mountain
a billy is a male goat

explanation.surface: A country bumpkin is compared to a goat on the peaks.
explanation.walkthrough: HILLBILLY is a US term for an unsophisticated rural person from the mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: A hayseed is an American slang term for a rustic yokel, the same sort of country person.

clue.text: A London court of noblemen

parts.note: points to the London district and exhibition centre named a court belonging to certain peers, so the noblemen are the first half of that place-name

explanation.surface: A London tribunal staffed by aristocrats.
explanation.walkthrough: Earls Court is a district of west London; 'court' suggests a law court, but it is part of the place-name, and the noblemen are the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: These peers rank above viscounts and give their title to a London district's court.

clue.text: Speech sound in Tswana's language?

indicators.note: the answer sits within the letters of the clue's last two words

explanation.surface: A sound heard in an African language.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters running through 'Tswana's language' actually give NASLA: the setter has swapped the last two, so the hidden word only works as NASAL with that slip allowed for.
explanation.definitionFit: Phonetics classes sounds such as m and n, voiced through the nose, as this kind of consonant.

clue.text: Middle-gear selected when overheating

parts.note: suggests changing into a mid gear when a car's engine runs hot, but means a garment for the middle of the body chosen in hot weather

explanation.surface: A driver picks a middle gear when the engine runs hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gear' means clothing, not a car's gears, and 'Middle' is the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: This simple wrap worn around the hips is the minimal clothing chosen in great heat.

clue.text: Wicked four in sea-trip

indicators.note: to trip is to stumble, so the letters of four, in and sea fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something evil involving four people on a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sea-trip' looks like a voyage, but 'trip' is the anagram signal and 'sea', with 'four' and 'in', is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Nefarious is a formal synonym for villainous, evil or criminal behaviour.

clue.text: Rivet in safe act to open?

indicators.note: suggests prising the words apart, so their letters are set out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wondering if a rivet in a safe is there to open it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rivet' is a verb here, meaning to hold the attention.
explanation.definitionFit: To rivet someone is to grip their attention completely, to enthral them.

clue.text: He found himself winning on the pools!

definitions.text: He found himself winning on the pools!

parts.words: He found himself winning on the pools!
parts.note: suggests a lucky football-pools gambler, but means the youth of Greek myth who fell for the reflection he found in a pool of water, finding himself winning in the sense of attractive

explanation.surface: A man discovers he has hit the jackpot on the football pools.
explanation.walkthrough: The football pools were a British betting game on match results; here the pools are water and 'winning' means charming.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this youth fell in love with his own face seen reflected in water.

clue.text: One of twin air-intakes below a bridge

definitions.text: One of twin air-intakes below a bridge

parts.words: One of twin air-intakes below a bridge
parts.note: suggests a pair of vents under a road bridge, but the bridge is the bony ridge of the nose

explanation.surface: A pair of ventilation shafts beneath a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The bridge is the top of the nose, with two openings below it.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the two nasal openings, through which we breathe, sits under the bridge of the nose.

clue.text: Type most commonly taking first-class return in European republic

parts.note: roman is the ordinary upright typeface, the one used most often

indicators.note: the first-class mark comes back to front

parts.note: A1 means first-class, read as the letters A and I

explanation.surface: A common typeface gets a first-class return ticket to a European country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first-class' is A1, read as AI, turned round by 'return' to IA.
explanation.definitionFit: Romania is a republic in south-eastern Europe.

clue.text: Letter to doctor for a lozenge

parts.note: rho is a letter of the Greek alphabet
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: Writing to one's GP about a throat sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lozenge' suggests a cough sweet, but here it is the diamond shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhomb, or rhombus, is the equal-sided diamond figure also called a lozenge in geometry and heraldry.

clue.text: Herb runs rings round daughter of Lear

indicators.note: the two rings go on either side of the daughter's name

parts.note: two rings look like two letter Os
Regan is one of King Lear's daughters in Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A man named Herb easily outdoes one of King Lear's daughters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' looks like a man's name, but it is the plant; 'runs rings round' is the idiom for outclassing.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is a culinary herb related to marjoram.

clue.text: Early days of Elizabethan favourite, as depicted by Millais

definitions.text: Early days of Elizabethan favourite, as depicted by Millais

parts.words: Early days of Elizabethan favourite, as depicted by Millais
parts.note: refers to the painting by Millais of young Walter Raleigh, a favourite of Elizabeth I, listening to a sailor's tales

explanation.surface: The youth of a royal favourite, as painted by a Victorian artist.
explanation.walkthrough: Millais's painting is The Boyhood of Raleigh; Sir Walter Raleigh was a favourite courtier of Elizabeth I.
explanation.definitionFit: Early days of a man's life are his youth, the title word of the Millais painting.

clue.text: French writer reversing into tree

indicators.note: the writer's name is read backwards, as a car goes into a space in reverse

parts.note: Albert Camus was a French novelist and philosopher

explanation.surface: A French author backs his car into a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumac is a shrub or small tree of the genus Rhus, grown for its foliage and spice.

clue.text: Hip-replacement recently? Hobby required!.

indicators.note: the letters of hip are put back in a different order, as in a hip operation

parts.note: taken as written
lately means recently

explanation.surface: Someone who has just had a hip operation needs a pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacement' rearranges HIP into PHI, the Greek letter, before LATELY.
explanation.definitionFit: Philately, stamp collecting, is the classic example of a hobby.

clue.text: Appeal to president to show the way

parts.note: to lead is to show the way

explanation.surface: Begging the president to give a lead.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead is to appeal earnestly, to beg or make an entreaty.

clue.text: Dramatic piece for violin

indicators.note: a piece of the word is taken, the answer being part of it

explanation.surface: A theatrical composition for a violin.
explanation.walkthrough: An Amati is a violin made by the Amati family of Cremona.
explanation.definitionFit: An Amati is a violin from the Cremona workshop, so the maker's name stands for the instrument.

clue.text: Children's writer making a fortune with English?

parts.note: a king's ransom is a fortune, so ransom stands for a huge sum

explanation.surface: An author for young readers getting rich with an English book.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ransome wrote Swallows and Amazons.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ransome is a classic English author of sailing stories for young readers.

clue.text: Brave to take a crack with a garden-tool, endlessly

parts.note: a rap is a sharp blow, as is a crack

indicators.note: the tool's name loses its final letter, cut off at the end

parts.note: a hoe is a garden tool for weeding

explanation.surface: A bold warrior has a go at something with a hoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts HOE to HO. 'Brave' is a noun here: a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: A brave is a Native American warrior, and the Arapaho are a people of the Great Plains.

clue.text: Behold Hated terribly

parts.note: lo is an old exclamation meaning look or behold

indicators.note: suggests the letters of hated are badly disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation drawing attention to something intensely disliked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' shuffles HATED into ATHED after LO; the whole clue also reads as 'hated terribly', meaning detested.
explanation.definitionFit: To be detested intensely is to be hated terribly, a stronger form of disliked.

clue.text: How like Heather to have one company in dire distress

indicators.note: the number and the firm are placed inside the shuffled word
puts the letters of dire into a damaged, disordered state

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A woman named Heather has a single business in serious trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distress' rearranges DIRE as ERID, and 'in' puts I and CO inside it. 'Heather' is the plant, not a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ericoid is a botanical adjective describing plants resembling heath, of the genus Erica.
